wrong.Form 10-K: The 10-K is the annual report, not the place for a press release.
wrong.No filing: Results can come out before the 10-Q or 10-K. But FINRA says an earnings press release must be filed on an 8-K with its text.

questions.simple: Form 8-K carries it, because a company that issues an earnings press release must file one with the release text.

reasons: SEC filing rule that can change over time

questions.q: Earnings season usually starts about two months after a calendar quarter ends.
questions.why: False. FINRA says earnings season typically begins in the first two weeks after the end of each quarter. That puts it in early to mid January, April, July and October. Schwab says it begins about two weeks after quarter end and lasts approximately six weeks.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the four seasons on your calendar. FINRA says they can be busy and volatile.
questions.simple: False, earnings season starts about two weeks after a quarter ends, not two months.

reasons: FINRA and Schwab agree; stable convention

questions.q: Management's guidance is one of the estimates averaged into the consensus.
questions.why: False. FINRA says the consensus is the average for all the analysts covering the stock. Nasdaq calls it the mean of their forecasts. Guidance is management's own forecast, not an analyst's estimate. Nasdaq notes management often gives guidance to try to direct the consensus to what is achievable. So guidance may steer the average, but it is not one of the numbers in it.
questions.lesson_line: Guidance tries to steer the consensus. The consensus itself is the analysts' average.
questions.simple: False, the consensus is only the analysts' average, and guidance comes from the company.

reasons: FINRA and Nasdaq agree (Nasdaq fact added)

questions.story: You hold a stock that is up 3R on the trade. It reports AMC tonight.
questions.q: Under our earnings rule, what's the plan?
questions.simple: Sell first, because our rule holds through earnings only when the trade is up 5R, and this one is up 3R.
questions.why: Sell before the news hits. Our rule: hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. This one is up 3R, short of that line. AMC means the company reports after the market has closed. A stop won't cap the loss: after a gap, the stop becomes a market order that may fill well below it.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R or more, you may hold through a report. Under that, be out before it.

wrong.Hold it through the report: Our rule holds through a report only when the trade is up 5R. At 3R, sell first.
wrong.Hold with a breakeven stop: A stop is a trigger, not a price. A gap can fill you well below it, and our rule still needs 5R.
wrong.Add shares before the report: Our rule bars new buys in the 3 days before a report. Buying more is a new buy.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting a breakeven stop. Schwab notes a report outside market hours can make a stock gap, with no trading in between. Our rule avoids the gap instead of hoping the stop holds.

questions.q: Our earnings rule bars a new buy today in a stock that reports AMC two days from now.
questions.why: True. Our rule bars new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Two days out is inside that window. AMC only means the results come after that day's close.
questions.simple: True, because our rule bars new buys in the 3 days before a report, and two days away is inside that.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Check the date and its BMO or AMC tag first.

reasons: days versus sessions is an open question elsewhere; two days is inside 3 under either reading

questions.story: You bought at $50 with a $45 stop, so you risked $5 a share. The stock now trades at $60, up 2R. It reports AMC tonight.
questions.q: What does our earnings rule say to do today?
choices: Sell before the report comes out
Sell half, hold the rest through it
Hold, since the trade is a winner
Hold with the stop at breakeven
questions.answer: Sell before the report comes out
questions.why: Sell before the report comes out. Our rule holds a trade through a report only if it is up 5R. This one is up 2R, so it does not qualify. AMC means the results land after the close, so today's regular session is your last one before them.
questions.simple: Sell before the report: our rule allows holding through one only when the trade is up 5R, and this is 2R.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R or more, you may hold through a report. Under that, be out before it.

wrong.Sell half, hold the rest through it: Holding half is still holding through. Our rule allows that only when the trade is up 5R.
wrong.Hold, since the trade is a winner: Being up is not enough. Our rule needs the trade up 5R before you hold through a report.
wrong.Hold with the stop at breakeven: A report outside market hours can make a stock gap past a stop. Our rule asks for 5R, not a tighter stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding because the trade is green. Reports outside market hours can make a stock gap. A stop price is only a trigger, so a gap can skip it.

conflicts: Gross margin naming: the SEC's Beginners' Guide says the dollar subtotal (revenue minus cost of sales) is called 'gross profit' or sometimes 'gross margin'. Nasdaq ('gross profit margin'), Fidelity, Investopedia and company releases (NVIDIA's '73.4%') use gross margin for the percentage. The file keys gross margin as the percentage, uses 'gross profit' for the dollar figure, and never offers 'gross profit in dollars' as a wrong answer.

Fidelity's Learning Center page 'What is price-to-earnings (PE) ratio?' (https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/pe-ratio, read 2026-11-09) states the forward P/E as estimates divided by price and says a forward P/E HIGHER than the trailing P/E suggests expected growth. That is backwards for the standard ratio (Nasdaq: today's price divided by consensus forecast earnings; Schwab and Investopedia agree; the same price over a bigger EPS gives a smaller multiple). The page is NOT cited; the forward-P/E scenario follows Nasdaq, Schwab, Investopedia and the arithmetic.

Float: what is excluded differs by source. Nasdaq: shares available to the public, excluding insiders and restricted stock. FINRA (public float): excludes officers, large stakeholders and governments. Investopedia: subtracts closely held shares (insiders, major shareholders, employees) and restricted stock; its worked example even removes large institutions. Keys use only the shared core (insiders' and restricted shares are out), and the float calculation's story labels the excluded shares as insiders' restricted shares. Investopedia's institutions example is not used.

Earnings season start: FINRA says it 'typically begins the first two weeks after the end of each quarter'; Schwab says it 'typically begins two weeks after the end of the quarter'. The true/false item keys 'about two weeks after', which both support.

Earnings surprise: Investopedia's definition says profits 'significantly' differ from expectations; FINRA and Zacks treat any difference from consensus as a beat or a miss, and Zacks gives the percent formula. Keys use the plain comparison with consensus and Zacks' formula.

BMO and AMC: no Tier 1 page found that spells out the abbreviations. FINRA (Tier 1) states the practice (companies usually report before the market opens or after it closes) and company releases show it (JPMorgan about 7:00 a.m. ET, Meta 'after market close'); the abbreviations themselves rest on Wall Street Horizon and Investing.com, two independent publishers documenting their own calendars. BMO is also Bank of Montreal's ticker; not used.

Implied move vs expected move: IBKR (Sosnick) says 'implied move', Schwab (Market Maker Move) and Cboe say 'expected move', and UCT's earnings card labels it 'Expected move'. Treated as one idea with two names; the implied-move item says so.

Whisper numbers: Investopedia notes some brokers have called the traditional broker 'whisper' a myth; FINRA and Schwab describe whisper numbers as real market expectations. Keys use only FINRA's description (an unofficial expectation that can differ from the consensus and become the market's expectation).

Regular trading hours (9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET) are from the SEC's Extended-Hours Trading bulletin as read 2026-11-09 (time-sensitive; exchanges have been working on longer sessions). Extended-session times vary by broker and are not quizzed.
Consensus figures differ by data provider. The NVIDIA beat and surprise items name LSEG's numbers as CNBC reported them ($1.25 expected); the surprise percent is computed from those two numbers only.
Market-cap size buckets (large, mid, small cap) differ by source (Investopedia uses $10 billion for large cap); not quizzed.

Low float and liquidity: the SEC staff's 2019 'Background Paper on the Market Structure for Thinly Traded Securities' reports a broker-dealer roundtable participant naming small floats as a main cause of low liquidity. That is a participant's view, not an SEC finding (and sec.gov refused the plain client), so it is not cited. q53 keys volatility (Nasdaq Tier 1, Investopedia agrees); wider spreads and hard entry and exit stay in its why as Investopedia's point only.
